title: Royce West says Texas' power shift could change what gets done next
text: Royce West says Texas’ power shift could change what gets done next Texas turned blue. Royce West says the focus now is delivering on affordability, health care and education priorities. The shift in political power in Texas also marks a major change for some of the state’s longest-serving lawmakers. After decades of working largely under Republican leadership in Texas, Democratic state Sen. Royce West believes his party has a new opportunity to deliver changes. In a one-on-one interview with NBC 5’s Brittney Johnson, West discusses the changes he believes Democrats will now have the power to pursue and what the shifting political landscape could mean for Texas. After decades of working largely under Republican leadership, Democratic state Sen.Royce West sat down one-on-one with NBC 5 Anchor Brittney Johnson to discuss the changes he believes Democrats will finally have the power to deliver.“There have been three days in my political life, I’ll put it that way, that have been very significant,” West said. “When I was first elected as a state senator. Secondly, when Barack Obama became president of the United States. And lastly, this past Tuesday, when Texas frankly turned blue.”For more than three decades, West has represented his Dallas-area district, spending much of that time with his party out of power.“The number of years I’ve been there, I’ve been a vice chair, I was a chairman, and then I became a vice chair, but little or no real input into what the agenda was for the committee consideration,” West said. “I get it, OK? And I wouldn’t wish that on no one else. ”“I passed legislation for body cameras,” West said.While proud of what Democrats have been able to accomplish, West said the party is now racing to get staff in place and tackle unfinished business, including health care. West pointed to Texas’ rate of uninsured residents, particularly children, and called health care one of his priorities for the next legislative session.“Health care issues, that has got to be one of our main objectives during this next legislative session, and hopefully Democrats and Republicans can come together,” West said. “I am filing a bill to do away with vouchers,” West said. “Our public school system is the system that we need to make certain that we continue to stand up.” West also hopes to kick off the upcoming legislative session by reinstating a procedural rule that would require lawmakers from both parties to work together.“It was called the two-thirds rule, which required Democrats and Republicans to work together,” West said. “I’m hoping that we can return to that particular rule. ” West sees something else historic in the state's new political leadership: women holding or potentially holding some of Texas' most powerful positions.“The governor is a woman. The lieutenant governor is a woman. And I’m hoping that the speaker ends up being a woman,” West said. Asked how having women in those three positions could influence the state's direction, West pointed to their experience and priorities.“They will bring, needless to say, their expertise as it relates to being skilled public servants. I didn’t say politicians, I said public servants,” West said.“And we’ll bring those in along with their priorities, and we’ll make certain that we come together and that the children, OK, don’t continue to squabble but come together. ” While the midterms shifted Texas from red to blue, West said one thing is clear: No matter who fills those seats, voters expect them to deliver on the issues that matter most.“The words don’t matter. The action matters,” West said.“And to the extent that we sit up and say we’re gonna deal with affordability, we had better deal with it. ” West encouraged Texans to remain engaged in the political process and hold elected officials accountable for keeping the promises that got them elected. West is also joining the Best Southwest Partnership to host a town hall focused on data centers on Nov. 14 at the University of North Texas at Dallas.
